Drivers consistently overestimate how much time they save by speeding. The effect is
well documented and it gets worse at higher speeds, which is exactly where the extra
risk is. Paceometer is a progressive web app that tries a different framing: instead of
a large speed number, it shows how many seconds you are behind an efficient pace for
the trip.

It started as a project a GW professor proposed to me. I have done the build and the
research, with him advising, and he is now seeking funding to bring it into his lab. It
is in pilot testing.

### What I did

- Designed and built the app in plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with all GPS
  processing kept on the device so no location data leaves the phone.
- Found that the original percentage-based trip metric inverted at highway speeds. It
  climbed toward 100 percent and in effect told drivers to go faster. I replaced it with
  a calculation of how many seconds you are behind an efficient pace, from the
  underlying `t = d / v` relationship.
- Ran a WCAG AA accessibility audit with Lighthouse and axe-core. I fixed contrast
  failures as low as 1.28:1 against a 3:1 minimum and added screen-reader
  announcements, labeled inputs, and reduced-motion support. The app now scores 100/100
  in Lighthouse with zero axe violations.
- Wrote the supporting literature review on time-saving bias, the link between speed and
  crash risk, and dashboard design. It keeps the parameters that come from published
  research separate from the design choices specific to this app.
